interactions.summary: Jiang asks what Dante means by deducing resurrection from the first parents, a student connects it to the immortality of the soul, and Jiang radicalizes the answer by saying the self is really an aspect of God that cannot die, only be reborn.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang question with student answer and Jiang restatement

interactions.summary: Jiang turns immortality into a challenge to modern goals like wealth and survival, and a student answers that Dante would reject happiness-as-maximization in favor of pursuing a spiritual good rather than material pleasure.

Jiang reopens the purpose-of-existence question, and a student offers a halting answer that God may have made humans as parts of himself that would bring him back, though the formulation remains confused.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang prompt with uncertain student speculation

speaker_notes.note: The student's answer is grammatically unstable and blends return-to-God language with a confused image of God coming back through humans.

claims.claim: A student interprets Dante's appeal to the first parents as a reaffirmation that the soul is immortal and survives corrupt flesh.
Jiang says the deeper message is that humans only think they are bodies, when in truth they are aspects of God, and that this makes them eternal.
Jiang argues that if the soul is truly eternal, then death is not the real problem because humans cannot finally die and can only be reborn.
Jiang uses this immortality claim to challenge modern life-goals centered on wealth, longevity, and fear of death.
A student says ordinary life may be about maximizing happiness without harming others, but also recognizes that Dante explicitly disagrees with that view.
The same student answers that Dante's real goal is not material pleasure but spiritual good, using the pilgrim's ascent through heaven while still in the flesh as evidence.
Another student speculates that God may have created humans as parts of himself meant to bring him back, but the answer remains conceptually unclear.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang tells the class that what they really are is not body or personality but an aspect of God itself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: what you are really is an aspect of God
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's strongest metaphysical compression and the reason death loses its finality in his reading.

signature_moments.moment: Modern commands to get rich and avoid death are mocked as beside the point once immortality is taken seriously.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Don't die. Don't die. But this is telling us, well, you weren't going to die anyway
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves Jiang's sharp collision between Dante's metaphysics and ordinary modern ambition.

signature_moments.moment: The student distills Dante's answer into a turn away from material pleasure and toward spiritual good.
signature_moments.source_phrase: we have to pursue not material pleasures, but a spiritual good
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet a clear practical consequence after Jiang's more abstract immortality argument.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A student's name for the end Dante points toward, contrasted with material pleasure and linked to ascent toward heaven.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet turns the resurrection passage into an existential reversal: if the soul is an eternal aspect of God, then the point of life cannot be mere survival or comfort but a movement toward spiritual good.

uncertainty_notes.note: The final student's answer is best treated as a confused speculation about return rather than a clean doctrinal claim, because the phrasing mixes God returning with humans bringing him back.
